mcqs.question: A product adds captions to all its videos, originally intended for permanently deaf users. Who else benefits, and why does this matter for prioritization?
options: Situational users, like someone watching on a train without headphones — because the same fix serves permanent, temporary, and situational impairments simultaneously
No one else benefits, since captions are a single-purpose accommodation
Only users with temporary hearing loss from an ear infection, not situational cases
Only users who have already enabled an accessibility setting in their OS
mcqs.explanation: The permanent/temporary/situational model shows the same accommodation typically covers all three groups at once — captions serve a deaf user and a headphone-less commuter identically, which is exactly why accessibility investment reaches a far wider audience than the specific group it was designed for. It isn't limited to temporary cases, and it works regardless of whether any OS accessibility setting is enabled.

mcqs.question: A user relies on a switch device rather than a screen reader. What does their experience of a page depend on most directly?
options: Whether alt text is present on every image
A correct, logical tab order and every interactive control actually being reachable via keyboard focus
Color contrast ratios across the interface
Whether the page has captions on any video content
mcqs.explanation: A switch device steps sequentially through focusable elements, so its usability depends entirely on tab order and keyboard reachability, not on alt text, contrast, or captions — those matter for other assistive technologies but aren't what a switch-device user's experience hinges on. This is exactly why different assistive technologies require genuinely different fixes.

mcqs.question: Why is there a real overlap between accessibility work and SEO, rather than the two being coincidentally similar?
options: Search engines directly penalize sites that fail WCAG audits
SEO tools automatically flag accessibility violations as ranking errors
Screen readers and search crawlers both depend on the same underlying signals — semantic structure, descriptive link text, meaningful alt text — so improving one tends to improve the other
Accessible sites load faster, and speed is the only shared factor between the two
mcqs.explanation: The overlap is structural: both a screen reader and a search crawler parse the same DOM and rely on the same signals — heading hierarchy, descriptive links, alt text — to understand a page, so fixing one for accessibility tends to help the other. There's no direct ranking penalty tied to a WCAG audit, and load speed is a separate (if sometimes correlated) factor, not the shared mechanism described here.

mcqs.question: A team assumes the ADA only applies to physical spaces like buildings and ramps, not to their web app. Why is that assumption risky?
options: The ADA was recently rewritten to explicitly exclude all software products
It only matters for companies with a physical retail location in addition to their app
It isn't risky — no accessibility law anywhere covers digital products, only physical ones
US courts have repeatedly extended ADA public-accommodation requirements to websites and apps, and thousands of web-accessibility lawsuits are filed annually
mcqs.explanation: Courts have repeatedly ruled that ADA public-accommodation obligations extend to digital products, and web-accessibility litigation under this framework is an active, well-established category with thousands of filings a year, not a physical-only requirement. There's no such exclusionary rewrite, other jurisdictions (EU, UK, Canada) have their own overlapping frameworks, and exposure isn't limited to companies with a physical storefront.

mcqs.question: Keyboard shortcuts, originally built for users who can't operate a mouse precisely, end up being adopted heavily by mouse-capable power users too. What does this illustrate?
options: The curb-cut effect — an accommodation built for one group often ends up benefiting a much wider group, changing the real ROI of the work
That keyboard shortcuts are a coincidence unrelated to accessibility design
That accessibility features usually only appeal to the narrow group they were designed for
That power users have an undiagnosed motor impairment
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook curb-cut effect: an accommodation designed for a specific accessibility need turns out to serve a much broader audience, which is exactly why treating accessibility work as narrowly scoped underestimates its actual value. It isn't a coincidence disconnected from accessibility, and it says nothing about the power users' abilities.

mcqs.question: A team adds `aria-label`s to every element and tests only with a screen reader, but their custom dropdown still can't be operated with the keyboard at all. What does this reveal about their approach?
options: That ARIA labels are unnecessary and should be removed
That the team is treating accessibility as synonymous with screen-reader support, missing keyboard-only users and switch-device users entirely
That the dropdown component itself is fundamentally impossible to make accessible
That the fix is to add more ARIA attributes rather than keyboard event handling
mcqs.explanation: This is the exact failure mode of collapsing accessibility down to whichever tool is most familiar — a component can be perfectly announced by a screen reader while remaining completely unusable by anyone relying on keyboard-only or switch-device interaction, which requires separate, non-overlapping fixes like proper focus and key handling. The dropdown isn't inherently impossible to fix, ARIA labels aren't the problem to remove, and more ARIA attributes alone won't add keyboard operability.
